publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The author suggests a plan for an MSc taught course structure incorporating an RF design exercise as one of its two-week-duration modules.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: At the University of Plymouth the Communication Engineering Group runs industrial postgraduate courses in RF design. These have been designed to meet the specific requirements of individual companies and carefully tailored to match the skills base of the attendees. The authors describe the approach to the design of these courses.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The teaching of high-frequency engineering at Bristol
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: Summary form only given. The manner in which Bristol University's Center for Communications Research has managed to attract higher quality students in relatively large numbers to undertake the Electronic and Communications Degree course with the inherent teaching of RF engineering is described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: RF expertise requirements at Nokia Mobile Phones (UK)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: Nokia Mobile Phones (NMP) are recruiting design engineers to resource the expanding number of products, but are finding it difficult to find let alone recruit, candidates with the right sort of skills required to develop current and next generation products. The author discusses the RF design skills NMP needs, and what it is doing to address the shortages in recruiting RF designers with these skills. He also suggests actions that the cellular engineering community can take to alleviate this shortage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The supply of radio engineers-survey results
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The author presents the results of a survey focused on undergraduate training. The results suggested that the total UK university output of graduate electronic engineers who are competent in radio engineering is less than 140/year, and of these, of course, many may choose other specialisations. The available supply is therefore probably less than 100 per year. The 7 responding industrial companies alone currently employ a total of 329 engineers whose work involves specialised RF knowledge, and, if it is assumed that the recruitment of RF engineers is in line with the average level of 9% of current staff, this would suggest an average annual recruitment need of 30 RF engineers for these 7 companies. This represents an unknown proportion of the total needs of UK industry, but it seems highly probable that it could be less than 30% of the total. The analysis supports the evidence of significant recruitment difficulty, but also suggests that a relatively modest increase in training levels, of say 50 RF engineers per year, would alleviate the problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Mobile Radio Training Trust: bridging the gap
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The author describes the work of the Mobile Radio Training Trust (MRTT), a charitable trust which serves both education and industry. The MRTT is concerned with overcoming the shortage of RF engineers with skills relevant to mobile radio.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: Marconi Instruments is involved in partnership with a small number of local schools. More generally the company has a long standing involvement with the Hertfordshire SATRO (Science and Technology Regional Organisation) which acts as a facilitator in encouraging various schools and businesses to get together and the newly formed Hertfordshire Education Business Partnership.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: Experience of running an MSc short course in RF Engineering currently in its seventh year is reported. The course has been consistently successful in attracting attendees from UK and European industry, in fact of the ten courses on offer it has been the most popular. The course is also an option for students enrolled for an MSc in Telecommunications and Information Systems at Essex.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: At Lund University RF techniques are taught on all academic levels in a fairly wide sense. Since there is good cooperation in both education and research with different companies within the Ericsson group (also on a personal basis), the courses are to some extent tailored to the needs of Swedish industry. The university has very good contacts in research with groups in Europe, but contacts with other European universities are being sought from the undergraduate students point of view of cooperation and exchange of students.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Satway: an assignment to introduce high frequency circuit design to undergraduates
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: Students can gain practical experience of the problems which arise with high frequency/RF design by using Satway, an exercise in analogue circuit design. The Satway exercise involves designing and building a circuit that allows a standard laboratory oscilloscope to display a standard 625-line television picture. To add interest to the exercise the signals used are received from the satellites currently transmitting television pictures to the UK and Europe.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The mismatch, in terms of quality and quantity, between the requirements of industry and the graduate output from academia with RF and microwave skills is well known. Collaborations between Middlesex University and industry have highlighted some of these problems and the authors address some of the principal issues relating to practical RF design. In particular, they discuss how RF theory and techniques can be taught with an emphasis on practical design, without compromising the rigorous mathematical treatment which is necessary for the proper development of the subject. A recent innovation at Middlesex is the teaching of RF and microwave technology through design tutorials rather than conventional lectures and this is discussed, together with other teaching methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Education in RF engineering-what the HEIs can offer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The author outlines the various mechanisms, both well established and novel, which exist in higher education institutes to promote the development of RF engineering skills in first and higher degree graduates.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radio frequency engineering: opportunity and challenge
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: RF engineering and products are in a phase of rapid evolution and development. The author briefly discusses the growth areas in RF engineering and emphasises the challenge presented to those involved in RF engineering education.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Skills and training requirements for RF engineers in industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: There is a severe shortage of RF design engineers with the necessary skills and experience to design the products required in the fast moving world of personal mobile communications. Although radio systems engineers are in short supply, the most acute shortage is being experienced by the manufacturers of base stations and radio terminals. Education and training needs are discussed and increased cooperation between industry, universities and other institutions is recommended.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The Teaching Company Scheme (RF engineering education)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The Teaching Company Scheme provides a possible mechanism which can be used in the context of education in RF engineering enabling the academic community to work more effectively with industry. The basis of the scheme is to establish a working partnership between the company and a university with the relevant expertise by developing and implementing a business plan or project via a high calibre graduate, an Associate. Historically the scheme has supported a wide range of activities such as management techniques, production processes through to total quality management, IT and marketing. Few programmes have been established to date building on the research work associated with RF engineering. The author confirms that the Teaching Company Scheme is available to support such work and also emphasizes the significance which is put on the education of the Associate within the programme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The distance learning approach (RF engineering education)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The authors set out a vision of the not too distant future where rapidly emerging technologies can facilitate distance learning in such a way that the personal development, and thus the industrial effectiveness, of RF engineers can be enhanced. The technologies to be used are those being developed for computer-supported cooperative working (CSCW) coupled with higher speed digital networks such as ISDN.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Projects in undergraduate and MSc courses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in RF Engineering
abstract: The author discusses the resources required for RF engineering projects for third or fourth year undergraduates and MSc students. The need for establishing good contacts with industry is emphasised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
